```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(featR)
```

## What featR is for

Feature selection in R is spread across a dozen packages, each with its own
calling convention and its own idea of what a result looks like. Comparing two
methods means learning two APIs and writing glue code to line up the answers.

featR wraps 14 selection methods behind one calling convention and one return
type, so swapping `fs_lasso()` for `fs_boruta()` is a one-word change. The
methods cover statistical filters, regularized and tree-based models, and
wrappers that refit a model per candidate subset. Two dimensionality-reduction
helpers, `fs_pca()` and `fs_svd()`, share the calling convention but not the
return type.

## Installing

The released version is on CRAN:

```r
install.packages("featR")
```

The development version is on GitHub:

```r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("elkronos/featR")
```

featR itself depends only on data.table, withr, and base R. The modeling
engines (glmnet, caret, Boruta, randomForest, brms, and others) are in
`Suggests`. A function that needs one checks when you call it and stops with
the `install.packages()` line you need.

## The calling convention

Every selection function takes the data first and the name of the outcome
column second:

```r
fs_<method>(data, target, <method options>, ...)
```

Housekeeping arguments come last. Every function takes `verbose`. Functions
that use randomness take `seed = NULL`, and functions that can run in parallel
take `n_cores`, `parallel`, or both. The four methods with no outcome,
`fs_correlation()`, `fs_unsupervised()`, `fs_pca()`, and `fs_svd()`, drop
`target`. `fs_svd()` calls its input `x`, because it takes a matrix rather than
a table of observations.

featR runs sequentially unless you ask for parallel workers, and caps any
request at the cores the machine has. It never touches your random number
generator unless you pass `seed`, and then restores the previous state when
the call returns. [Reproducibility and
parallelism](https://elkronos.github.io/featR/articles/reproducibility.html) has the details.

Every selection function returns an `fs_result`, and `selected()` pulls the
kept feature names out of any of them. `fs_pca()` and `fs_svd()` reduce
dimensions rather than choose variables, so they return their own
decomposition lists instead.

## A worked example

This example predicts `mpg` in `mtcars` from the other ten columns. It uses
two filters, both of which run with no suggested packages installed.

`fs_supervised()` scores each feature against the target on its own: absolute
Pearson correlation when the target is numeric, a one-way ANOVA F statistic
when it is categorical. The two scales differ (|r| runs from 0 to 1, F has no
upper bound), so a threshold that suits one is meaningless for the other. Keep
the features with |r| above 0.5:

```{r}
relevant <- fs_supervised(mtcars, target = "mpg", threshold = 0.5)
relevant
```

Eight of the ten columns pass. `gear` (|r| = 0.48) and `qsec` (0.42) fall
below the cut. The scores sit in `relevant$scores`:

```{r}
round(sort(relevant$scores, decreasing = TRUE), 2)
```

A filter that looks at one feature at a time cannot see that two survivors
carry the same information. `cyl` and `disp` both score 0.85 here, and they
are correlated 0.90 with each other. `fs_correlation()` ignores the outcome and
looks only at how the features relate to one another. With `prune = TRUE`, the
default, it drops features one at a time until no remaining pair is correlated
above the threshold:

```{r}
pruned <- fs_correlation(mtcars[, selected(relevant)], threshold = 0.8)
pruned$details$dropped
```

It dropped `cyl` and `disp`. `summary()` shows the call and a ranked score
table, with an asterisk on each feature that was kept. For `fs_correlation()`,
a feature's score is its largest absolute correlation with any other input
feature, dropped ones included. That is why `wt` (0.89 with `disp`) and `hp`
(0.83 with `cyl`) score above 0.8 and still survive, because their partners
were dropped.

```{r}
summary(pruned)
```

`selected()` returns the final set, ready to pass to a model:

```{r}
keep <- selected(pruned)
keep
fit <- lm(reformulate(keep, response = "mpg"), data = mtcars)
```

`fs_supervised()` looked at `mpg` to choose these six columns, so any error
estimate for `fit` computed on the same 32 rows is optimistic. Run the
selection on training rows only and score the model on rows it never saw.
[Validation and leakage](https://elkronos.github.io/featR/articles/validation-and-leakage.html) shows how, and
lists which numbers featR reports are honest held-out estimates.

To try another method, change the function and its options. With glmnet
installed, the lasso version of the same question is:

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("glmnet", quietly = TRUE)}
lasso <- fs_lasso(mtcars, target = "mpg", seed = 1)
selected(lasso)
```

[The fs_result object](https://elkronos.github.io/featR/articles/fs-result.html) covers the seven components,
what `scores` means for each method, and how to compare results side by side.

## The four families

| Family | Functions | Guide |
|---|---|---|
| Filters | `fs_unsupervised()`, `fs_supervised()`, `fs_correlation()`, `fs_chi()`, `fs_infogain()` | [Filter methods](https://elkronos.github.io/featR/articles/filters.html) |
| Regularization and embedded importance | `fs_lasso()`, `fs_elastic()`, `fs_randomforest()`, `fs_mars()` | [Regularization and embedded importance](https://elkronos.github.io/featR/articles/regularization.html) |
| Wrappers | `fs_recursivefeature()`, `fs_svm()`, `fs_boruta()`, `fs_stepwise()`, `fs_bayes()` | [Wrapper methods](https://elkronos.github.io/featR/articles/wrappers.html) |
| Dimensionality reduction | `fs_pca()`, `fs_svd()` | [Dimensionality reduction](https://elkronos.github.io/featR/articles/dimensionality-reduction.html) |

## Where to go next

If you are not sure which function fits your data, start with [Choosing a
method](https://elkronos.github.io/featR/articles/choosing-a-method.html). It pairs common questions with
functions and has a table of what each function accepts: task type, data
types, missing values, and which suggested package it needs.

Before you report any number from a selection, read [Validation and
leakage](https://elkronos.github.io/featR/articles/validation-and-leakage.html). The full list of functions and
arguments is in the [reference](https://elkronos.github.io/featR/reference/index.html).
